pr_title: esp32/machine_hw_spi: Use a 2 item SPI queue for long transfers.
pr_body: Using a 2-item transaction queue instead of 1 allows long transfers to be executed with the minimum inter-transaction delay. Limit maximum transaction length to ensure an integer multiple of the SPI `bits` setting are transferred. Fixes #7511.
pr_comments:
This change looks pretty good to me.  If I understand it correctly then anyone using SPI with `bits=` 8, 16, 24, 32 will see no change if byte length <= 4092, and will see reduced gaps between chunks if byte length > 4092.

For other multiples of `bits`, the gap between chunks will now occur at a slightly different location (a `bits` boundary), and the gap will be smaller.

So +1

> This change looks pretty good to me. If I understand it correctly then anyone using SPI with `bits=` 8, 16, 24, 32 will see no change if byte length <= 4092, and will see reduced gaps between chunks if byte length > 4092.

Yes. In fact it's kind of worse with the current implementation for long transfers as the inter-transaction delays can cross a word boundary so you might have been half way through one of those 16/24/32 bits and suddenly been hit with a huge gap.

> For other multiples of `bits`, the gap between chunks will now occur at a slightly different location (a `bits` boundary), and the gap will be smaller.
> 
> So +1

Yes, odd word sizes will have a slightly reduced maximum single transaction size, but shorter gaps for long transfers and always between words.

>  In fact it's kind of worse with the current implementation for long transfers as the inter-transaction delays can cross a word boundary so you might have been half way through one of those 16/24/32 bits and suddenly been hit with a huge gap.

Is that true? 8/16/24/32 all divide evenly into 4092*8 bits.

> Is that true? 8/16/24/32 all divide evenly into 4092*8 bits.

Oh yes, sorry, that is of course true! It's only odd word sizes that would have caused problems.
Actually, hold off on this for a moment: I was just testing with the len <= 4 case and I'm getting IDF errors – even though I've not touched that code.

OK. False alarm. I keep forgetting that I'm using `bits=72`. I tried to send a 3 byte buffer and it threw errors. Digging into this it's – of course – because the length is rounded down to a multiple of `bits`, which turned out to be `0`. Trying to send 0 bits causes Bad Things to happen.

I've added a check for this and am throwing a `ValueError`. Just returning without executing a transfer would be semantically correct, but I felt that this is almost certain to be a mistake and something that the user would want to know about. This is a code path that most people wouldn't get near I don't think. I'm happy to change it to a return if you think that's more in-keeping with other functionality.

> I've added a check for this and am throwing a `ValueError`.

That looks OK.  I don't think any other port has a specific check for zero length and it may be undefined behaviour on them.  Can revisit this if needed in the future.

issue_context.title: ESP32: hardware SPI with long transfers has (relatively) large inter-transaction delays
issue_context.body:
The hardware SPI on ESP32 only supports individual transactions up to 4092 bytes, so long transfers must be executed as a number of individual transactions. This works OK, but the gap between the transactions is relatively long.

I'm (as usual) abusing the ESP32 hardware and using SPI to generate WS281x-style pulse-width-modulated data streams (basically generate an expanded bitstream where 100 is a zero and 110 is a one). Since this is a single-wire, self-clocking protocol, those gaps disrupt the stream and cause flickering on pixels that lie beyond the 4092-byte boundary. This limits the maximum pixel chain length to 454 GRB pixels (or 341 GRBW).

I assumed that this was unavoidable, but a bit of time reading the IDF documentation and scanning the code has made me realise that MicroPython is using a single item transaction queue for the hardware SPI and awaiting each transaction individually. By switching to a 2-item queue and ensuring there's always a transaction ready for when the in-flight one finishes (combined with explicitly acquiring and releasing the SPI bus around all of the transactions), this inter-transaction delay can be reduced to the point where it doesn't disrupt the data stream.

I've got a fairly ugly draft PR in place for doing this (#7510). I'm going to conduct a few more tests and then submit it for consideration.
comments:
Ooh! It's good, but not *quite* good enough. It looks like it only works reasonably reliably if the inter-transaction delay occurs exactly between two pixels and starts to fall apart around 3 transactions.

4092 bytes represents *exactly* 341 of my GRBW pixels here, so I get a pretty solid 682 pixels. I'd say that's a worthwhile improvement, but the fact that it's not going to work reliably on GRB pixels makes me hesitate to call this a win…

So if I limit the transaction size to a maximum of 4068 bytes, I get a neat 452 GRB pixels or 339 GRBW pixels. That'd mean I could drive up to 904 GRB pixels on one chain pretty reliably (I'm gonna lose the stream if a higher priority interrupt hits around the inter-transaction gap).

This feels like a worthwhile improvement for a few lines of diff, but it's too hacky for mainline so I don't think I'll submit that PR. I'm gonna leave this bug open for a bit in case anyone else has some thoughts to chip in.

I realised the neat way to make this non-hacky: if we use the `bits` field of the SPI object to indicate the word size of the data transfer then we can align the maximum transaction size to this (actually the lowest common multiple of this and 8 bits so we don't have to do any crazy bit shifting on the subsequent transactions).

So I can just use `bits=24*3` or `bits=32*3` when initialising the SPI object to indicate whether these are GRB or GRBW pixels and have an appropriate transfer size. Inter-transaction gap should be ~25µs according to the IDF docs, which is short enough to avoid a WS281x frame end. So it's flicker-free as long as you don't get an interrupt hit over the transaction boundary.

Have updated my PR and will tag as ready for consideration.

review_comments: what does this actually do, does it allocate internal memory for both queues?  what about the `len <= 4` case in `machine_hw_spi_transfer` below, is that ok that it still uses 1 queue?

This is a good question. The IDF documentation just says:

> Transaction queue size. This sets how many transactions can be ‘in the air’ (queued using `spi_device_queue_trans` but not yet finished using `spi_device_get_trans_result`) at the same time.

I am assuming that it something to do with memory allocation, but I assume the queue is just pointers to the transaction structures, so I can't imagine it being that big a deal.

For small transfers, these still count as a single transaction item in the queue, it's just that the bits are stored straight in the transaction instead of being a pointer. So, yes, small transfers will still use 1 queue item.
can you please make this a loop rather than recursive, just in case the compiler cannot eliminate the tail recursion
Sure. I was being lazy here and just grabbing the first/simplest GCD implementation I could find. I wasn't sure if I'd be instructed to actually put it somewhere else as a utility function.
